source.title: Sparse Autoencoders Learn Monosemantic Features in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Mateusz Pach; Shyamgopal Karthik; Quentin Bouniot; S. Belongie; Zeynep Akata

record.file_problem: The full paper is present. There are occasional PDF extraction and layout artifacts, but the relevant text and tables are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests neuron-level semantic mixing with a newly proposed image-similarity measure rather than the original studies' methods. It also compares raw model neurons with SAE latents and varies SAE settings.
record.gate_note: The paper measures image-similarity-based monosemanticity (MS) for original vision-model neurons and SAE neurons, and reports results for width, sparsity, SAE type, and image encoder. The steering experiments demonstrate the use of SAE features, but do not measure how often or strongly unmodified models exhibit polysemanticity. Cited claims about polysemanticity and superposition are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study's raw-neuron baselines bear on V1. Original neurons in four pretrained vision encoders (CLIP ViT-L, SigLIP, AIMv2, WebSSL MAE) score MS 0.01, against up to 1.00 for SAE latents. That means their activating images are no more similar than chance, a different method from the originals' feature visualization. Most other rows score SAE latents. SAE latents are a post-hoc dictionary built by the study, not the model's own neurons, so they do not bear on V5. The human study validates the metric.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that SAEs on VLM vision encoders make individual units far more monosemantic than the original neurons by their MS score, which matches human judgments. Sparsity and width matter most, and Matryoshka SAEs score best. Best-unit MS rises with width, but overall MS peaks near ε=4 and then falls. SAE units can steer LLaVA outputs. Raw neurons are described as polysemantic, a point the paper takes from prior work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a new activation-weighted pairwise image-similarity score and compares original neurons with SAE latents; it does not reproduce the original studies' neuron-analysis method.
record.method_sensitivity: MS results vary with SAE width and sparsity; overall MS can decline at very wide widths, and human-score alignment varies with the MS difference and image encoder used to compute embeddings.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE latents trained on fixed vision-encoder activations score far higher MS than raw units, even at equal width (×1: 0.57-0.86 best). MS rises with width and sparsity at a reconstruction cost (R2 31.3% at K=1 to 74.9% at K=50).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse dictionary learning on a vision encoder's activations yields units more monosemantic than the encoder's own neurons, even at equal width.

fits_no_version.finding: Human choices of the more focused top-16 image grid agree with MS in 82.8% of pairs. Agreement rises from about 56% for small MS gaps to 100% for gaps of 0.8-0.9, nearly the same with either embedding encoder.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-weighted image-embedding similarity tracks human judgments of neuron monosemanticity.

record.problems: MS is an image-embedding similarity proxy for semantic focus, not a direct test that the activating inputs are unrelated or that the network uses no shared feature. The reported best-neuron values do not characterize the typical neuron; the paper provides additional distributional plots and summary statistics, but some are figure-based. The steering evaluation does not test downstream capability retention.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within the 60-row limit, omitted most per-layer and per-expansion-factor entries in Table 1a and the detailed average/best/worst MS tables A2-A7, as well as additional curve points in Figures 5, A6-A9 and detailed user-study bins in Table A1. The retained rows prioritize raw-neuron comparisons, representative width and sparsity outcomes, cross-encoder/model results, and human alignment results.

untested.parts: CNN image classifiers such as InceptionV1 and their specific neurons (e.g. cat faces / car fronts) are not studied. Raw units are residual-stream/CLS dimensions of ViTs, not activation-function neurons. MS shows activating images are dissimilar, but cannot show they lack a shared feature.
Superposition is only cited as an explanation; feature count vs neuron count is never tested as a cause.
No tests of initialization, regularization or training noise.
The model's activation function, architecture and training are never varied. SAEs are post-hoc decompositions of fixed activations, so the share of polysemantic model neurons is not shown to change.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not reassessed.

Activation-range cutoffs are not varied. Swapping the embedding encoder shifts absolute MS (raw 0.01 with DINOv2 vs 0.48 with CLIP ViT-B) but leaves the SAE-over-raw ordering unchanged. No neuron is shown changing classification.

missing.what: Raw-neuron MS with CLIP ViT-B as the embedding encoder: mean about 0.48 across layers, best 0.50 / worst 0.47, i.e. near the encoder's chance floor, vs SAE means 0.52-0.63.
SigLIP SoViT-400m raw-neuron MS across layers 11/16/21/last with CLIP ViT-B: mean about 0.48, best 0.49-0.54.
Raw-neuron mean MS 0.0135 with std ≤0.0004 at every CLIP layer (No SAE 0.01 ± 0.00 in Table A11): all raw units uniformly at chance.

record.verdict_notes: Neither original source is among this study's authors. The raw 'neurons' are basis dimensions of the CLS residual stream or projection output, which have no privileged basis. Near-chance MS is expected there, and it speaks weakly to V1's claim about classifier neurons. MS weights the whole activation range after min-max normalization, so it cannot separate unrelated mixtures from broad weak activation. The reader's V5 links were wrong: SAEs do not change the model's neurons. The V7 links were also wrong: the human study validates the metric rather than showing that status depends on measurement.

versions.untested_parts: Measures similarity among images activating neurons, not the specific InceptionV1 neuron or examples in the claim, and does not establish that the distinct activating images lack any shared feature.
No transformer-language-model MLP neurons or language inputs are studied.
The paper mentions superposition as a possible explanation but does not test whether feature count exceeds neuron count or whether that causes the measured mixtures.
Does not test initialization, regularization or training noise as causes of polysemanticity when capacity is sufficient.
Tests SAE type, latent width, and sparsity in selected vision encoders. It does not test SoLU, modern convnets, or whether downstream model capability is retained without a large loss.
Does not reassess canonical neurons such as InceptionV1 4e:55 with tools to establish that their apparently mixed inputs share a feature.

Compares image-embedding encoders used for MS and reports agreement with human judgments at different score gaps. It does not vary activation-range cutoffs or explanation-scoring methods beyond these comparisons.

labels.reason: The best raw unit scores MS 0.01 in every layer and model (Tables 1a, 1b), and the text calls these units polysemantic (Fig 1). Caveats: the units are residual or output dimensions, not neurons, and the encoders are not classifiers.

relation.reason: Raw-neuron MS is measured as a control and bears on V1, though the paper's focus is SAE evaluation.

tranche.reason: A different method (an activation-weighted pairwise-similarity MS) applied to the same question, whether neurons respond to unrelated inputs. Raw neurons serve as the baseline.

source_check.notes: The raw-unit result is the No-SAE baseline of an SAE paper, and the MS metric is new with no stated chance level. Every raw unit gets the same score (std <=0.0004; 0.47-0.50 with CLIP ViT-B). That fits min-max-normalised dense activations, where MS tracks the mean image similarity rather than top-image content. This is an inference: the paper does not discuss it. Rows r29-r32 repeat the V1 number next to SAE values.

statements.correction: CLIP ViT-L: CLS residual stream after layers 11/17/22/23 plus final projection output; best = worst MS 0.01, mean 0.0135 (Tables 1a, A2, A5). SigLIP, AIMv2, WebSSL: highest raw-unit MS 0.01, worst not reported (Table 1b). E = DINOv2 ViT-B. No chance level stated.
statements.problem: The numbers, layers and models are right. 'Best = worst' is shown only for CLIP ViT-L (Tables A5, A11). For SigLIP, AIMv2 and WebSSL the text gives only the best unit. The text never states a chance level. For the non-CLIP encoders the units are final-layer CLS tokens, or two random token embeddings where there is no CLS token, and the text does not say which.

statements.correction: The encoders are CLIP, SigLIP, AIMv2 and WebSSL MAE, which are pretrained vision encoders, not classifiers.
The units are CLS-token residual-stream dimensions or final projection outputs (CLIP). In the other encoders they are final-layer CLS or random token embedding dimensions.
statements.problem: For CLIP the units are CLS residual-stream dimensions or final-projection outputs. For the other encoders they are CLS or random-token dimensions, and the text does not say which.

statements.correction: Highest raw-unit MS is 0.01 in all five CLIP ViT-L layers (r1-r5; best = worst, Table A5) and in the last layer of all four encoders (r29-r32, Table 1b).
statements.problem: The rows cited for 'four ViT encoders' are r1-r5, but those are the CLIP ViT-L layers. The four-encoder rows are r29-r32. 'Every unit at 0.01' is shown only for CLIP ViT-L. For the other three encoders the text gives only the best unit (0.01). It never calls 0.01 chance.

statements.correction: CLIP ViT-L raw units with E = CLIP ViT-B: mean MS 0.4812-0.4840 (Table A3), best/worst 0.50/0.47 (Table A6). With E = DINOv2 ViT-B: best = worst 0.01 (Table A5). SAE gains are smaller ('less distinctively') with CLIP ViT-B (App. E.2). Human AS is within 0.04 across the two encoders in every MS-distance bin (Table A1, e.g. 0.56 vs 0.60, 0.81 vs 0.77).
statements.problem: The text gives no chance level. 0.48 is not a floor either: with CLIP ViT-B, the worst SAE units score 0.06 to 0.41 (Table A6). Human alignment barely changes with the encoder: per-bin AS differs by at most 0.04 (Table A1).

statements.correction: Raw units in four ViT encoders have highest MS 0.01. The text calls them polysemantic: Fig 1, and the intro says one fires from 'cellphones to rulers'.
statements.problem: For this study, only ViT-encoder units with low MS are cited. The text calls original neurons polysemantic only in passing (Fig 1 and intro).
